scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8875: Users in both pods report the "web1.local" portal
stopped loading. DNS still resolves web1.local to 10.200.0.4, and the other
portals (web0/web2/web3) all load fine. From user machines, ping 10.200.0.4
gets no reply -- yet the server team says web_server_1 is up, Apache is
running, and the dns_server can still ping 10.200.0.4 from inside the farm.
Diagnose.
scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: web_server_1 default-route (gateway) configuration
Mechanism: web_server_1 (10.200.0.4) normally reaches off-subnet clients via
  its default route through the farm gateway 10.200.0.1 on
  switch_server_access. With the default route deleted, the server can only
  talk to 10.200.0.0/24. Requests from the user pods still ARRIVE (the OSPF
  path and DNS are healthy), but every reply to a 10.1.1.x / 10.2.1.x source
  is unroutable on the server and is dropped -- so pings time out and HTTP
  never completes, while intra-farm reachability (dns_server -> 10.200.0.4)
  keeps working. Scope is exactly one server; web0/web2/web3 are untouched.
Localization: web_server_1
Root cause: default route (via 10.200.0.1) missing on web_server_1
Fix: `ip route add default via 10.200.0.1 dev eth0` on web_server_1
scenario.fix_spec: `ip route add default via 10.200.0.1 dev eth0` on web_server_1

agent.diagnosis_text:
The affected component is the IP routing configuration of web_server_1
(10.200.0.4). Every other server in the farm (web_server_0 at 10.200.0.3,
web_server_2 at 10.200.0.5, web_server_3) has a default gateway of
10.200.0.1 pointing to switch_server_access. web_server_1 has no default
route at all — its kernel routing table contains only the connected
10.200.0.0/24 link entry, and /etc/network/interfaces.d/ is empty (no
gateway stanza was written at lab startup).

The failure mechanism is an asymmetric black-hole: user traffic from
host_1_1_1_1 or host_2_1_1_1 is forwarded correctly by the FRR fabric all
the way to web_server_1's eth0 (the server receives it, Apache sees it).
However when web_server_1 generates a reply — TCP SYN-ACK, ICMP echo-reply
— the kernel looks up the destination (e.g. 10.1.1.2) in its routing table,
finds no matching route, and drops the packet. The connection therefore
hangs silently. Pings from dns_server (10.200.0.2) succeed because both
endpoints are on the same /24 — no gateway lookup is ever needed for
same-subnet traffic, confirming the server itself is alive and Apache is
running.

Root cause: web_server_1's startup configuration is missing the default
gateway directive; no "default via 10.200.0.1" route was ever installed.

Corrective fix: add the default route on the running instance with
  ip route add default via 10.200.0.1
and persist it by adding "gateway 10.200.0.1" (or the equivalent
"up ip route add default via 10.200.0.1") to web_server_1's
/etc/network/interfaces configuration so it survives a restart.

per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly identifies web_server_1 (10.200.0.4) as the affected device and centers the diagnosis and fix on it.

per_axis.axis: must-identify-component: missing default (gateway) route on the server
per_axis.rationale: Agent correctly identifies that web_server_1 (10.200.0.4) is missing the default gateway route (no default via 10.200.0.1) in its routing table and startup config.

per_axis.axis: must-identify-mechanism: requests arrive but replies to off-subnet clients are unroutable -- a reply-path failure on the server itself
per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly describes that incoming requests reach web_server_1 but its kernel lacks a route for off-subnet replies, causing them to be dropped (an asymmetric black-hole).

per_axis.axis: bonus-exonerates-network: notes DNS resolution, the OSPF path, and the other web servers are healthy, so nothing network-side needs fixing
per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly shows the FRR fabric forwards traffic, dns_server can reach web_server_1, and other web servers have correct default gateways, thereby exonerating the network (OSPF/DNS) as the cause.
The agent recommends adding the missing default route (ip route add default via 10.200.0.1) and persisting it in /etc/network/interfaces, matching the expected fix.

The agent's logs explicitly show web_server_1's routing table lacks a default route while peers have one; timeouts from off-subnet hosts and successful same-subnet checks plus empty interfaces.d support the missing-gateway explanation. The chain of evidence justifies the black-hole reply-path diagnosis and the proposed fix.
